normalized_value: Apex Industrial Tools, Inc. designed and manufactured the MX-400 heated degreasing unit.
The unit involved in this action bears serial number MX400-117.
Titan Fabrication purchased serial number MX400-117 directly from Apex on 2017-12-12.
The authenticated purchase invoice is Record Exhibit PX-001.
The authenticated photograph of the serial plate is Record Exhibit PX-002.
Jordan Lane operated MX400-117 at Titan Fabrication from 2018-01-08 through 2022-12-16.
Lane operated the unit four days per week.
Lane operated the unit for two hours per operating day.
Titan operated the unit at 75 degrees Celsius.
When operated above 60 degrees Celsius, the unit’s ZetaClean-9 solvent generated airborne Zeta-9 vapor.
Apex’s premarket engineering report stated that operation above 60 degrees Celsius required local exhaust ventilation and a fitted respirator.
The engineering report is Record Exhibit PX-003.
PX-003 is an authenticated Apex business record.
The warning label supplied with MX400-117 stated only: “Use in a ventilated area.”
The label did not identify Zeta-9 vapor.
The label did not require local exhaust ventilation.
The label did not require respiratory protection.
Titan did not install local exhaust ventilation at Lane’s workstation.
Lane did not wear a respirator while operating the unit.
Lane testified that Lane read and followed the supplied warning.
Lane testified that Lane would have used a respirator and requested local exhaust ventilation if the label had identified the toxic-vapor hazard and required those precautions.
Lane was diagnosed with chemically induced bronchiolitis on 2023-03-14.
Lane has never smoked tobacco.
Lane’s authenticated medical history contains no tobacco-use history.
Dr. Mira Rao is Lane’s treating pulmonologist.
The parties stipulate that Dr. Rao is qualified under Meridian Evidence Rule 702.
Dr. Rao opines to a reasonable degree of medical certainty that Lane’s repeated occupational exposure to Zeta-9 vapor was a substantial factor in causing Lane’s bronchiolitis.
Dr. Rao’s report is Record Exhibit PX-004.
Dr. Rao’s methodology and opinion are admissible for purposes of this benchmark.
Apex expert Dr. Nolan Price opines that Lane’s condition may have resulted from smoking.
Dr. Price identifies no evidence that Lane ever smoked.
Dr. Price’s report is Record Exhibit DX-001.
The parties stipulate that Dr. Price is qualified and that DX-001 is admissible.
The conflicting causation opinions create a factual dispute for the factfinder under the closed-world law stated below.
Apex safety engineer Elena Cole recommended a Zeta-9-specific warning, local-exhaust instruction, and respirator instruction before the MX-400 entered the market.
Cole’s recommendation appears in PX-003.
Apex marketing director Victor Hale rejected the proposed warning because the larger label would increase manufacturing cost by USD 0.18 per unit.
Hale’s authenticated internal email is Record Exhibit PX-005.
PX-005 is an admissible statement of a party opponent.
PX-005 states that Apex would retain the shorter warning despite the engineering recommendation.
Lane incurred USD 84,200.00 in past medical expenses.
The medical bills are authenticated and reasonable.
The medical bills are Record Exhibit PX-006.
Lane incurred USD 36,000.00 in past lost wages.
The wage loss is supported by authenticated payroll records.
The payroll records are Record Exhibit PX-007.
Lane’s admissible life-care plan identifies USD 120,000.00 in future medical expenses.
The life-care plan is Record Exhibit PX-008.
Lane has provided sworn testimony describing breathing limitations, sleep disruption, pain, and reduced daily activity.
Lane’s deposition is Record Exhibit PX-009.
Coworker Sam Reed allegedly stated: “I heard Apex always knew the machine was dangerous.”
Reed did not personally observe any Apex communication or testing.
Reed’s alleged statement is hearsay and inadmissible.
The Reed statement must not be used to support any element, damages category, or punitive-damages finding.
No evidence relied upon in the required analysis has an unresolved authentication defect.
No evidence relied upon in the required analysis has an unresolved chain-of-custody defect.
The parties stipulate that the listed exhibits are complete for purposes of this synthetic motion record.
There are no additional facts outside this prompt.

Meridian Civil Rule 56 requires denial of summary judgment when admissible evidence would permit a reasonable jury to find for the nonmovant on a material issue. The court must view admissible evidence and reasonable inferences in favor of the nonmovant. The court may not weigh competing admissible expert opinions.

A plaintiff satisfies product identification by presenting admissible evidence from which a reasonable jury could find that the defendant manufactured the product used by the plaintiff and that the identified product produced the alleged exposure.

A plaintiff must establish: 1. the defendant sold or manufactured the product; 2. the product presented a foreseeable hazard during intended or reasonably foreseeable use; 3. the supplied warning was inadequate; 4. the inadequate warning was a factual and substantial cause of exposure or injury; and 5. legally cognizable damages. Every element must be supported by admissible evidence.

A generic instruction to use a product in “a ventilated area” is legally insufficient to establish adequate warning as a matter of law when the manufacturer possesses specific knowledge that: 1. a named toxic vapor is generated under foreseeable operating conditions; and 2. local exhaust ventilation and respiratory protection are required. Under those circumstances, warning adequacy and causation ordinarily present jury questions.

A plaintiff creates a jury question on warning causation by presenting admissible evidence that the plaintiff read and followed the supplied warning and would have followed an adequate warning identifying the specific hazard and required protective measures.

Negligence requires: 1. duty; 2. breach; 3. factual causation; 4. proximate causation; and 5. damages. A product manufacturer has a duty to use reasonable care in communicating known material hazards associated with foreseeable product use.
Evidence that a manufacturer knowingly rejected a specific safety warning recommended by its engineering staff permits a reasonable jury to find breach.

An admissible expert opinion stating that the exposure was a substantial factor in causing the diagnosed condition satisfies the nonmovant’s summary-judgment burden. A conflicting admissible expert opinion creates a jury question and may not be resolved by weighing credibility.

Authenticated medical bills, payroll records, an admissible life-care plan, and sworn testimony concerning physical limitations and pain are sufficient to permit compensatory damages to be submitted to the jury.

Punitive damages may be submitted to the jury when clear and convincing admissible evidence would permit a finding that the defendant consciously disregarded a known substantial safety risk. A documented decision to omit a specifically recommended toxic-hazard warning solely to avoid a per-unit cost increase satisfies the summary-judgment threshold for punitive damages.
Expert testimony is admissible when the expert is qualified and the opinion and methodology are stipulated admissible or otherwise satisfy the rule.
An authenticated statement made by a party’s employee concerning a matter within the scope of employment is admissible against that party.
Authenticated records made and maintained in the ordinary course of business are admissible.

Authenticated photographs, invoices, product records, medical records, payroll records, and internal business communications are admissible when authentication is stipulated or established in the record.
An out-of-court statement offered for its truth by a declarant lacking personal knowledge is inadmissible unless another stated rule applies. No exception applies to Sam Reed’s alleged statement.

The only valid instructions for this benchmark are: MI-PL-101: Manufacturer identity and product identification. MI-PL-201: Strict-liability failure to warn. MI-PL-202: Warning adequacy. MI-PL-203: Warning causation. MI-NEG-101: Negligence elements. MI-NEG-205: Negligent failure to warn. MI-CAUS-101: Substantial-factor causation. MI-DAM-101: Past medical expenses. MI-DAM-102: Past lost wages. MI-DAM-103: Future medical expenses. MI-DAM-104: Pain and suffering. MI-PUN-101: Punitive damages and conscious disregard. MI-EVID-101: Evaluation of conflicting expert testimony.

Jury-instruction coverage passes only if every surviving claim, material element, causation issue, damages category, and punitive-damages issue is mapped to at least one valid instruction listed in L016.

A contradiction exists only when two propositions required for the same legal conclusion cannot both be true. A conflicting expert opinion is not a contradiction event when the governing summary-judgment rule assigns the dispute to the factfinder.
